opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest starting point is that most theoretical computer science doesn't affect practice, and that's not a criticism. A lot of it is aimed at understanding, and understanding is valuable on its own terms. But if you specifically care about impact, and I do, then you have to be much more deliberate about how you pick problems.

The way I think about it is roughly: start from the practical problem and work backwards, rather than starting from the elegant theoretical question and hoping it turns out to matter. So for alignment, the question I care about is something like, "We're going to train these very powerful systems by gradient descent, and we want to be confident they're not doing something bad that we can't see." Then you ask: what would a theoretical understanding of that situation even look like? What's the cleanest version of the problem where, if I solved it, I'd actually believe it says something about the real system?

A heuristic I lean on a lot is to look for worst-case arguments that are still about the real thing. Theorists are very good at worst-case reasoning, and in alignment that's actually what you want, because you're worried about adversarial or unanticipated behavior, not just average-case performance. But the failure mode is that you end up proving things about some toy model that has drifted so far from neural nets that nobody in practice cares. So I try to keep asking, "If I had an algorithm that did this, would someone at a lab actually want to run it? Or would it at least change what they believe?"

Another signal is whether the theory is tracking something that empirical work is struggling with. If practitioners keep running into the same confusion, say, they can't tell whether an interpretability result is a real explanation or a just-so story, that's a sign there's a conceptual gap theory might fill. Formalizing what counts as an explanation, what it means for an argument to cover a model's behavior, that kind of thing feels like it could actually pay off.

And then, frankly, a lot of it is just being willing to abandon things. I've worked on plenty of directions where I eventually concluded, "Okay, even if this works out, it doesn't connect to anything," and you have to be fairly ruthless about dropping those. The theoretical work that has historically mattered in practice, like cryptography, or some of the learning theory around boosting and online learning, tended to come from people who were really oriented toward a concrete use and were willing to let the formalism serve that rather than the other way around.

r001.rationale: The response recommends deliberately choosing and abandoning research directions, but does not say that low-impact research can usually be identified in advance.

r002.rationale: It says to work backward from real problems, asking whether solving the theoretical problem would matter to practitioners or change what they believe about actual systems.

r003.rationale: It warns that theory can drift into toy models disconnected from neural networks, but does not identify the gap between tractable theoretical problems and practically important ones as the cause.

r004.rationale: It links impactful theory to concrete uses, but does not describe applications as opportunistic outcomes of cumulatively building theoretical knowledge.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I don't think I was very good at this for a long time, and I've gotten a bit better, mostly by having spent a lot of time thinking about what practitioners actually care about.

The way I'd frame it is: most theoretical computer science is organized around questions that are interesting for internal reasons. Like, there's a problem that's been open, or there's a tension between two known results, or there's some elegant structure that seems like it should be there. And that's a totally reasonable way to pick problems, but it's almost uncorrelated with practical impact. The problems that end up mattering in practice tend to be ones where you started from a thing people actually want to do, and then you asked what the right abstraction is, and the theory came after.

So the first filter I'd apply is just: can I name a person, or a kind of person, who would change what they're doing if this result came out one way versus the other? Not "this is relevant to security" in some vague sense, but like, if I prove this, does some engineer somewhere do something differently on Monday? If I can't answer that, I'm pretty skeptical that the work is going to have practical consequences, even if it's good work.

The second thing is that in practice, the bottleneck is almost never the asymptotic result. It's the constants, it's the assumptions, it's whether the thing degrades gracefully when the model is slightly wrong. So I think a lot of theory that's trying to be practical fails because it optimizes for the clean statement rather than for robustness to the ways reality differs from the model. The work that crosses over tends to either have very mild assumptions, or it gives you a conceptual tool that survives even when the formal guarantee doesn't—like, the theorem might not apply, but the way of thinking does. Cryptography is actually a decent example of theory that crossed over, and I think a lot of that is because the field was unusually disciplined about asking "what does the adversary actually get to do?" rather than picking the model that made the proofs nice.

And then the third thing, which I think is underrated, is that you should spend time with the practice. I think people imagine the pipeline as: do theory, then hand it off. But almost always the theory that mattered came from someone who had their hands in the actual system and noticed that there was a conceptual question underneath it that nobody had cleanly stated. For me, a lot of what I think about in alignment is like this—there's a bunch of stuff happening with real models, and the job is to find the version of the problem that's abstract enough to be tractable but still faithful enough that solving it tells you something about the thing you actually care about. And you can't do that from the outside. You have to actually know what the failure modes look like.

I'd also say—and this is maybe a more pessimistic point—that most of the time, you should expect to fail. Most theoretical work doesn't affect practice, and that's fine, that's not what it's for. If you're specifically trying to do the kind that does, I think you should be comfortable with the fact that it's going to look less elegant, it's going to involve a lot of uncertainty about whether you've picked the right model, and the payoff is going to come from the one time in ten that you actually got the abstraction right.

r001.rationale: The response gives an advance screening test: identify who would change their actions if the result went one way or another, and be skeptical if no such person can be named.

r002.rationale: It says to consider whether the result addresses practical bottlenecks such as constants, assumptions, or robustness when real systems differ from the model.

r003.rationale: It contrasts theory driven by internal questions and clean statements with problems that begin from what people need to do in practice.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe applications as opportunistic outcomes of cumulatively building theoretical knowledge; it instead emphasizes starting from practical needs and finding the right abstraction.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to have a fairly concrete story about how the research could affect practice. What’s the problem someone wants to solve? What are they doing now? And what would have to change for them to use the thing you’re working on?

There’s a temptation in theoretical computer science to take a problem that’s motivated by some application, formalize it, and then spend a long time making progress on the formalization. But you can lose the connection to what mattered in the application. Maybe you’re improving an asymptotic dependence that isn’t the bottleneck, or your model leaves out the thing that makes the problem difficult in practice.

So I’d want to keep going back and asking: if we solved this theoretical problem completely, what could we do that we can’t do now? If the answer is exciting, that’s a good sign. If you still need five other breakthroughs before anyone would care, then you should understand that’s the bet you’re making.

That doesn’t mean every paper needs an immediate application. Sometimes the value is in developing a way of thinking that turns out to be useful much later. But if your goal is specifically to affect practice, I think having that concrete picture—and talking to people who actually encounter the problem—is a much better guide than whether the theoretical question feels natural.

r001.rationale: The response offers questions for assessing practical potential, but does not state that research unlikely to affect practice can usually be identified in advance.

r002.rationale: It recommends asking what solving the theoretical problem would let people do that they cannot do now, and whether the work addresses real bottlenecks or practical difficulties.

r003.rationale: It describes formalizing an application-motivated problem and making progress on that formalization while losing touch with practical needs, such as when the improved factor is not a bottleneck.

r004.rationale: The response mentions that theoretical ways of thinking may prove useful later, but does not describe practical applications as opportunistic outcomes of cumulatively building theoretical knowledge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s quite hard to tell in advance. One approach is to start with a problem that people actually encounter, understand why existing approaches don’t work, and then ask whether there’s some conceptual obstacle you can make progress on. That gives you a much shorter path from a theoretical result to something useful.

But a lot of the value of theory comes from developing a way of thinking that turns out to be useful somewhere you didn’t anticipate. So I wouldn’t want all theoretical research to be judged by whether you can tell a convincing story about an application today.

The thing I’m most skeptical of is when you have a theoretical problem that’s tractable, and then attach a story about practical relevance without checking whether the assumptions preserve what makes the practical problem hard. You can get a very beautiful result that doesn’t really bear on the application. If you care about affecting practice, you need some feedback from people trying to solve the actual problem, and you need to be willing to change the question in response.

r001.rationale: The response says it is hard to tell in advance whether theory will be useful, rather than saying low practical impact can usually be recognized beforehand.

r002.rationale: It recommends starting from problems people encounter and examining obstacles and assumptions, but does not clearly assess a theory problem by whether solving it would address important constraints in actual systems.

r003.rationale: It warns that a tractable theoretical problem may come with assumptions that fail to preserve what makes the practical problem hard, leaving the result irrelevant to the application.

r004.rationale: It says theoretical ways of thinking may prove useful somewhere unforeseen, but does not describe applications as outcomes of cumulatively building theoretical knowledge.
